claims.text: Adding approximately 2–5 at.% boron to phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve their glass-forming ability.
Adding approximately 2–5 at.% boron will increase the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous phase.
The targeted phosphorus-containing alloys are conventionally marginal glass formers.
The targeted alloys are prone to crystallization at typical cooling rates.
The beneficial effect should occur under rapid-cooling processes such as melt spinning.
The beneficial effect requires sufficiently low boron concentrations for boron to remain dissolved in the amorphous matrix without forming separate boron-rich phases.
Boron modifies local atomic packing by inducing atomic-size mismatch.
Boron modifies chemical short-range order and enhances topological and chemical disorder.
Boron is small relative to the other alloy constituents and can form strong, directional bonds.
Boron-induced packing and bonding changes frustrate the nucleation of crystalline phases.
Frustrated crystal nucleation raises the kinetic barrier to crystallization.
A higher kinetic barrier to crystallization produces a deeper supercooled-liquid region and greater amorphous-state thermal stability.
Relative to a boron-free baseline, boron-containing alloys will have a higher critical cooling rate for glass formation.
Relative to a boron-free baseline, boron-containing alloys will form glass under slower cooling conditions.
Relative to a boron-free baseline, boron-containing alloys will exhibit a higher crystallization-onset temperature in differential scanning calorimetry.
Above approximately 5 at.% boron, the improvement may diminish or reverse.
Excess boron may cause phase separation or formation of boron-rich crystalline compounds.
The magnitude or direction of the boron effect may depend on the phosphorus-containing base-alloy composition.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome calls for a higher critical cooling rate while interpreting it as glass formation under slower cooling. The falsification rule instead treats a reduced critical cooling rate as the expected improvement. Glass formation under slower cooling corresponds to a lower, not higher, critical cooling rate.
